note: Analyst Shark, security angle only. Findings judged against the North Star; severities not inflated for non-tracing issues. The reviser changelog is non-substantive (15× “Applied a search/replace patch”) and is not treated as evidence that security gaps were closed.

findings.section: Phase 0 (profile fixture); Phase 1 (transcripts); Phase 2 (trace schema / EXECUTION-LOG)
findings.criterion: Nothing in this effort ships to v1.1.x collaborators
findings.message: The plan deliberately captures and commits the exact materials that hold credentials—real v1.2 profile state including cookies and localStorage, capability transcripts from curl/CLI/REPL against a live environment, and end-to-end traces whose required fields include `capability_call` arguments plus network method/URL/response. It never defines a redaction policy, a secret-class inventory, a non-shared store for evidence, or a gate that fails if auth headers, API keys, session cookies, or bearer tokens appear in artifacts under the Foreman tree. Shared-artifact ledger rows cover DB/config/static/endpoints, not evidence blobs. Without fail-closed secret hygiene, wave commits and collaborator-visible paths can ship live auth material to v1.1.x collaborators—or leave “isolation” as a ledger story while secrets travel through the same git history the plan otherwise polices.

findings.section: Phase 3/4 — Attach induced-fault set; Doctor forced-failure fixture
findings.criterion: open/run/stop/restart including Doctor diagnose and session attach without a dead control; every health/usage/diagnose surface works end-to-end or fails with a named state
findings.message: Acceptable faults include “revoked credential,” “wrong key,” and “bogus session ID” against John’s real v1.2 environment, but the plan never requires an isolated credential fixture, a pre-fault snapshot, or a post-fault restore attestation. A GREEN wave can permanently revoke or overwrite the live keystore, after which Diagnose and Attach become dead or stuck in auth-failure for all subsequent work and for S1—exactly the dead-control / broken-diagnose failure the North Star forbids. “Forced failure proves the diagnostic is real” without a restore contract is a security test that can destroy the product surface under test.

findings.section: Phase 0 shared-artifact ledger; Phase 2 cost_state migration; Phase 3/4 per-wave shared-artifact checklist
findings.criterion: Nothing in this effort ships to v1.1.x collaborators
findings.message: Isolation is “named per artifact” and collaborator smoke runs only after a wave already reports a modified shared artifact. That is detect-after-write, not prevent-before-write. There is no hard gate that blocks the first migration, static deploy, or schema write when the ledger row’s isolation mechanism is unproven, STUB, or absent—and no fail-closed default if a feature flag is missing, inverted, or ignored by a code path. Feature-flagged-off for v1.1.x is stated as prose, not as a pre-flight proof that a v1.1.x process cannot see the new column, route, or asset. The North Star’s collaborator clause fails the first time a wave writes under a false isolation claim; a later smoke check cannot unship a shared DB change.

findings.criterion: Doctor diagnose works end-to-end or fails with a named, user-visible state (not theater); nothing ships secrets/behavior to collaborators via shared surfaces
findings.message: The handoff payload is required to carry “raw signal” (plus issue id, engine, timestamp) into Doctor with a test that it pre-selects the issue. The plan never bounds what “raw signal” may contain, never forbids embedding full auth errors, token fragments, env dumps, or command lines with secrets, and never requires redaction before render or persistence. A diagnose path that “works” by dumping credential material into UI, logs, or shared session storage is both a security defect and an honesty defect: the surface claims diagnosis while leaking the means of account takeover, and any shared storage of that payload can violate the collaborator isolation clause.

findings.criterion: session attach without dead control; named failure states (unknown ≠ empty ≠ zero); Retry re-issues a viable action or explains why not
findings.message: `unauthorized` appears in the reason enum and “revoked credential” is an induced fault, but acceptance never requires session-binding or authz checks: that Retry may not re-issue across principal boundaries, that unauthorized must not collapse into timeout/unknown_session (security-relevant misclassification), and that attach traces prove the capability refused the wrong identity rather than only returning a typed string. Without that, an attach/retry control can look honest in UI while being a security-dead or security-liar control—retrying under the wrong session, or classifying auth failure as a recoverable transport problem—undermining the attach honesty and dead-control clauses.

findings.section: Phase 0 cost_state ↔ branch-isolation; Phase 2 cost_state enum migration
findings.criterion: Cost never fabricates dollars; nothing ships to v1.1.x collaborators
findings.message: The plan allows an additive nullable `cost_state` column with backfill defaulting to `unmeasured`, “feature-flagged off for v1.1.x,” and only asks plan-time whether the column is acceptable under isolation. It does not require a concrete negative test: a v1.1.x reader must not observe new columns/routes/labels, and a flag-off path must not render dollar figures from partial backfill. A migration that lands in a shared database with defaults of `unmeasured` while v1.1.x still infers labels from numeric zero either fabricates cost semantics for collaborators or ships schema they never consented to. Isolation resolution as a written opinion is not a security control.

findings.section: Phase 1 new-window renderer split; Phase 3/4 Preview wave content-classification
findings.criterion: File preview shows human-friendly documents; binary no longer dumps as text; no raw-binary preview
findings.message: Classification is magic-byte + content-type + size ceiling, resolving to named states. There is no path-sandbox rule (open only under allowed roots), no denial of symlink/escape, and no policy for active content (macros, embedded scripts, PDF JS) when reusing “native browser viewer” or an in-repo conversion path. A path-escape or hostile document can force the shared preview path into undefined behavior—raw dump, empty mislabel, or crash that presents as a dead/broken control—or process files outside the user’s intended project. The North Star’s raw-binary and honest-preview criteria are incomplete without a fail-closed open boundary; size and magic bytes alone are not a security boundary.

findings.section: Phase 0 collaborator smoke-check protocol; Phase 3/4 per-wave shared-artifact line
findings.criterion: Nothing in this effort ships to v1.1.x collaborators
findings.message: Smoke is defined as a named collaborator check after modification, logged in EXECUTION-LOG. That is useful detection, not prevention. Combined with Finding 3, the plan still lacks a pre-merge / pre-wave isolation proof and a HALT that forbids further waves until a failed collaborator check is rolled back or renegotiated. Relying on post-facto human smoke for a North Star hard constraint treats collaborator contamination as an audit finding rather than a ship-blocker at the moment of write.

findings.criterion: Handoff hygiene / nothing ships unintended changes affecting collaborators; controlled write surface for the build
findings.message: The smoke test’s success criterion is that a stage2 cwd can edit a repo-root file. That proves the run can touch paths outside the planning directory—including shared manifests and assets the collaborator ledger cares about—yet the plan does not require a subsequent write-allowlist or path policy for product waves. Security of the build harness is left at “containment works or we move cwd,” which expands blast radius for accidental shared-artifact writes rather than narrowing it. This is a refinement of isolation/hygiene, not a general multi-tenant hardening ask.
